item.title: “Furthermore, monks, one sees that woman’s corpse thrown in a charnel ground — with skeleton still connected, still having flesh and blood, held together by…
item.description:
“Furthermore, monks, one sees that woman’s corpse thrown in a charnel ground — with skeleton still connected, still having flesh and blood, held together by sinews … with skeleton still connected, without flesh but smeared with blood, held together by sinews … without flesh, without blood, held together by sinews … disconnected bones scattered here and there — here a hand bone, here a foot bone, here a shin bone, here a thigh bone, here a hip bone, here a back bone, here a skull. What do you think, monks? Has her former charm and beauty disappeared and peril become evident?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Thus, monks, is the peril in the case of forms.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 13 – Mahādukkhakkhandhasutta

item.title: “Sunakkhatta, I give this simile to make the meaning clear. The meaning here is this: The wound, Sunakkhatta, is a synonym for the six sense-bases…
item.description:
“Sunakkhatta, I give this simile to make the meaning clear. The meaning here is this: The wound, Sunakkhatta, is a synonym for the six sense-bases (phassayatana). The poison, Sunakkhatta, is a synonym for ignorance. The dart, Sunakkhatta, is a synonym for craving. The probing tool, Sunakkhatta, is a synonym for mindfulness. The knife, Sunakkhatta, is a synonym for noble wisdom. The surgeon, Sunakkhatta, is a synonym for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Indeed, Sunakkhatta, a monk who guards himself in regard to the six sense-bases, knowing that ‘Attachment (upadhi) is the root of suffering,’ becomes unattached and liberated by the destruction of attachment. It does not happen that he would still focus his body on attachment or direct his mind to attachment.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 105 – Sunakkhattasutta

item.title: “Monks, just as a skilled carpenter or his apprentice might use a small peg to knock out, drive out, and remove a larger peg; so…
item.description:
“Monks, just as a skilled carpenter or his apprentice might use a small peg to knock out, drive out, and remove a larger peg; so too, monks, when a monk attends to some sign and gives attention to it, if evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, ill-will, and delusion arise, then that monk should attend to a different sign connected with what is wholesome, not that sign. By attending to a different sign connected with what is wholesome, those evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, ill-will, and delusion are abandoned and subside. With their abandonment, the mind becomes steadied, settled, unified, and concentrated.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 20 – Vitakkasaṇṭhānasutta

item.title: “Householders, those venerable ascetics and brahmins do not see the peril, the degradation, the defilement of unwholesome states, nor the escape, the benefit, and the…
item.description:
“Householders, those venerable ascetics and brahmins do not see the peril, the degradation, the defilement of unwholesome states, nor the escape, the benefit, and the purification of wholesome states.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 60 – Apaṇṇakasutta

item.title: - What binds the world? By subduing what is one freed? By abandoning what thing Are all bonds destroyed? - Wish binds the world, By…
item.description:
- What binds the world?
By subduing what is one freed?
By abandoning what thing
Are all bonds destroyed?
- Wish binds the world,
By subduing sensual desire one is freed,
By abandoning wish,
All fetters are destroyed.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.69

item.title: “To what extent, Venerable Gotama, is the Dhamma visible here and now, immediate, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be directly experienced by the wise?” -…
item.description:
“To what extent, Venerable Gotama, is the Dhamma visible here and now, immediate, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be directly experienced by the wise?” - “Brahmin, being infatuated by craving, overwhelmed, with mind obsessed, one plans for one’s own harm, plans for others’ harm, plans for the harm of both, and experiences mental suffering and mental distress. When craving is abandoned, one does not plan for one’s own harm, nor for others’ harm, nor for the harm of both, and does not experience mental suffering or mental distress. Being infatuated by craving, brahmin, overwhelmed, with mind obsessed, one engages in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, misconduct of mind. When craving is abandoned, one does not engage in misconduct of body, speech, or mind. Being infatuated by craving, brahmin, overwhelmed, with mind obsessed, one does not know as it actually is one’s own benefit, nor the benefit of others, nor the benefit of both. When craving is abandoned, one knows as it actually is one’s own benefit, the benefit of others, and the benefit of both. Thus, brahmin, the Dhamma is visible here and now, immediate, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be directly experienced by the wise.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.54

item.title: “And what, monks, is the origination of the world? Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With…
item.description:
“And what, monks, is the origination of the world? Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling. With feeling as condition, craving. With craving as condition, clinging. With clinging as condition, existence. With existence as condition, birth. With birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. This is the origination of the world. Dependent on the ear … on the nose … on the tongue … on the body … Dependent on the mind and phenomena, mind-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling. With feeling as condition, craving. With craving as condition, clinging. With clinging as condition, existence. With existence as condition, birth. With birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. This, monks, is the origination of the world.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.107

item.title: “One who finds no core among becomings, Like one picking flowers from a fig tree — That monk abandons the near and far shore, Like…
item.description:
“One who finds no core among becomings,
Like one picking flowers from a fig tree —
That monk abandons the near and far shore,
Like a serpent sheds its worn-out skin.”

“One in whom there is no anger inside,
Who has gone beyond existence and non-existence —
That monk abandons the near and far shore,
Like a serpent sheds its worn-out skin.”

“One whose thoughts have been dispersed,
Internally well-ordered, without remainder —
That monk abandons the near and far shore,
Like a serpent sheds its worn-out skin.”

From: Sutta Nipāta 1.1

item.title: “One who restrains evil intent, Seeing the beautiful with sharp desire — That person’s craving increases; He makes the fetter strong.” “One who delights in…
item.description:
“One who restrains evil intent,
Seeing the beautiful with sharp desire —
That person’s craving increases;
He makes the fetter strong.”

“One who delights in calming the mind,
Always contemplating foulness, mindful —
That person will destroy craving;
He cuts off Māra’s fetter.”

“One who has reached the goal, without fear,
Free from craving, without defilement,
Having pulled out the dart of existence —
This body is his last.”

From: Dhammapada 334-359

item.title: Greed, hatred, delusion — these three, Are evil minds for a person, They damage one’s own self, They produce one’s own self, Like the rind…
item.description:
Greed, hatred, delusion — these three,
Are evil minds for a person,
They damage one’s own self,
They produce one’s own self,
Like the rind and core of a tree,
Producing its own fruit.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.2
